title: Naive Bayes & Probabilistic Classification
description: Bayes' theorem in classification, the naive conditional independence assumption, Gaussian NB, Multinomial NB, Bernoulli NB, and Laplace smoothing.

sections.title: Naive Bayes Classifiers
sections.subtitle: Fast, Probabilistic Classification Powered by Bayes' Rule and the Independence Assumption

sections.title: Bayesian Classification Formulation
sections.content:
Given a feature vector $\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d]^T$, we want to find the class $y \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ that maximizes the posterior probability $P(y | \mathbf{x})$:

$$P(y | \mathbf{x}) = \frac{P(\mathbf{x} | y) P(y)}{P(\mathbf{x})} \propto P(y) P(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d | y)$$

Computing the full joint likelihood $P(x_1, \dots, x_d | y)$ requires estimating $2^d$ parameters, which is computationally intractable.

sections.title: The 'Naive' Conditional Independence Assumption
sections.content:
Naive Bayes makes the simplifying assumption that **all features are conditionally independent given the class label $y$**:

$$P(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d | y) = \prod_{j=1}^d P(x_j | y)$$

The classification decision rule is therefore:
$$\hat{y} = \arg\max_y \left[ P(y) \prod_{j=1}^d P(x_j | y) \right] = \arg\max_y \left[ \ln P(y) + \sum_{j=1}^d \ln P(x_j | y) \right]$$

sections.title: The Three Primary Naive Bayes Variants
sections.content:
| Variant | Feature Modality | Likelihood Model $P(x_j|y)$ | Standard Industry Use-Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gaussian NB** | Continuous numeric features | Gaussian PDF: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$ | Sensor readings, biometric measurements |
| **Multinomial NB** | Discrete count data | Multinomially distributed word/token counts | Document classification, bag-of-words text |
| **Bernoulli NB** | Binary presence/absence | Bernoulli trial: $p_j^x (1-p_j)^{1-x}$ | Keyword presence in spam, short message tagging |

sections.title: The Zero Frequency Problem & Laplace Smoothing
sections.content:
If a word appears in the test document that never occurred in training class $y$, $P(\text{word} | y) = 0$. Because the likelihood is a product, **a single zero multiplier wipes out all other evidence and sets the entire probability to zero!**

**Remedy: Laplace (Additive) Smoothing:**
$$P(x_j = w | y) = \frac{N_{yj} + \alpha}{N_y + \alpha |V|}$$
Setting $\alpha = 1.0$ guarantees no word ever receives a probability of zero.

sections.title: Why Naive Bayes Works Surprisingly Well
sections.content: Even when the conditional independence assumption is mathematically violated in practice, Naive Bayes often produces surprisingly accurate **classification boundaries**, because finding the maximum posterior class requires only the correct ranking, not perfectly calibrated probabilities.

code.description: Train GaussianNB on continuous features, and MultinomialNB with Laplace smoothing on text data using Scikit-learn.
code.starter:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB, MultinomialNB
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# 1. Gaussian Naive Bayes on Continuous Data
iris = load_iris()
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(iris.data, iris.target, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)
gnb = GaussianNB()
gnb.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f'GaussianNB Iris Test Accuracy: {gnb.score(X_te, y_te)*100:.2f}%')

# 2. Multinomial Naive Bayes on Text with Laplace Smoothing (alpha=1.0)
corpus = [
    'free lottery cash prize winner claim',
    'quarterly revenue financial budget forecast',
    'claim your free luxury gift card now',
    'please review the attached report and spreadsheet'
]
labels = [1, 0, 1, 0]  # 1: Spam, 0: Ham

vec = CountVectorizer()
X_text = vec.fit_transform(corpus)
mnb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0)  # Laplace smoothing
mnb.fit(X_text, labels)

test_doc = ['free meeting schedule']
pred = mnb.predict(vec.transform(test_doc))[0]
probs = mnb.predict_proba(vec.transform(test_doc))[0]
print(f'\nTest Document: "{test_doc[0]}"')
print(f'Predicted: {"SPAM" if pred==1 else "HAM"} (Probabilities: Ham={probs[0]:.3f}, Spam={probs[1]:.3f})')

quiz.question: What is the core 'naive' assumption made by the Naive Bayes classifier?
options: All data points are normally distributed
All features are conditionally independent of each other given the class label: $P(x_1, \dots, x_d | y) = \prod P(x_i | y)$
The dataset has zero missing values
quiz.explanation: Naive Bayes assumes that given the class label, the presence or value of one feature is conditionally independent of any other feature.

quiz.question: What catastrophic numerical problem occurs when a word in a test document never appeared in training class $c$ without smoothing?
options: The estimated probability $P(\text{word}|c) = 0$, causing the entire product of probabilities to collapse to zero regardless of all other words
The model assigns 100% confidence to class $c$
quiz.explanation: Because probabilities are multiplied, a single zero probability forces the overall class likelihood to zero.

quiz.question: What technique is used to prevent zero probabilities in Naive Bayes?
options: Laplace (additive) smoothing (adding a pseudo-count $\alpha > 0$ to word counts)
quiz.explanation: Laplace smoothing adds a constant $\alpha$ (typically 1.0) to numerators and $\alpha |V|$ to denominators, ensuring all probabilities $> 0$.

quiz.question: In Scikit-learn's `MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0)`, what does `alpha=1.0` represent?
options: Laplace smoothing parameter (pseudo-count added to each category)
quiz.explanation: The `alpha` parameter controls additive smoothing; `alpha=1.0` is standard Laplace smoothing.

quiz.question: Which variant of Naive Bayes is designed for continuous real-valued features?
quiz.explanation: Gaussian Naive Bayes models continuous features by assuming each class feature follows a 1D normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu_{cj}, \sigma_{cj}^2)$.

quiz.question: Which variant of Naive Bayes is designed for discrete count data (e.g. word frequency counts in text documents)?
quiz.explanation: Multinomial Naive Bayes models discrete occurrence counts of tokens across a vocabulary.

quiz.question: Which variant of Naive Bayes is designed for binary boolean features (0 or 1, word present or absent)?
quiz.explanation: Bernoulli Naive Bayes models the presence or absence of features as independent binary Bernoulli trials.

quiz.question: Why is taking the logarithm of probabilities (log-likelihood) standard in Naive Bayes implementations?
options: To make the code run in fewer lines
Multiplying hundreds of small probabilities ($< 0.01$) causes floating-point underflow; log transforms products into stable sums: $\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b$
Because logarithms only work on positive numbers
Because log-likelihood is a neural network
quiz.explanation: Underflow occurs when multiplying many small fractions; summing logarithms prevents numerical precision collapse to zero.

quiz.question: What is the prior probability $P(y = c)$ in Naive Bayes typically estimated as?
options: The relative frequency of class $c$ in the training dataset: $\frac{N_c}{N}$
The inverse of the number of features
quiz.explanation: Class priors are estimated directly from empirical class frequencies in the training dataset.

quiz.question: How does Gaussian Naive Bayes estimate $P(x_j | y = c)$ for a continuous feature $x_j$?
options: By computing the class mean $\mu_{cj}$ and variance $\sigma_{cj}^2$ from training data and evaluating the Gaussian probability density function at $x_j$
quiz.explanation: Gaussian NB computes sample mean and variance for each class-feature pair and evaluates the normal PDF.

quiz.question: Is Naive Bayes considered a generative or discriminative model?
options: Generative, because it models the joint probability distribution $P(x, y) = P(x|y)P(y)$ and can generate synthetic data
quiz.explanation: Naive Bayes is generative because it models how the data was generated $P(x|y)$ alongside class priors $P(y)$.

quiz.question: How does Naive Bayes compare in training speed to Logistic Regression and SVMs?
options: Naive Bayes is exceptionally fast because training requires only a single pass through data to compute counts, means, and variances ($O(N \cdot D)$)
quiz.explanation: Naive Bayes has closed-form statistical parameter estimates (frequencies and means), requiring no iterative optimization.

quiz.question: Why does Naive Bayes perform well on text classification (e.g. spam filtering) despite the independence assumption being obviously false (words depend on context)?
options: Because words are actually independent in English
Classification only requires that the correct class has the highest relative posterior probability ranking, not that probabilities are accurately calibrated
Because Naive Bayes uses transformers internally
quiz.explanation: Domingos & Pazzani showed that even when probability calibration is distorted by correlation, the decision boundary often preserves optimal ranking.

quiz.question: What happens when features in a dataset are highly correlated in Naive Bayes?
options: The code will crash with an error
Correlated features are counted redundantly, causing the model to overconfidently exaggerate the posterior probability toward 0 or 1
quiz.explanation: Redundant correlated features act like duplicate votes, multiplying evidence repeatedly and distorting probability magnitude.

quiz.question: What is Complement Naive Bayes (CNB) designed to address in Scikit-learn?
options: Severe class imbalance in text classification by utilizing statistics from the complement of each class
quiz.explanation: Complement Naive Bayes estimates parameters from the complement of each class, making it superior for imbalanced text classification.

quiz.question: Can Naive Bayes handle streaming data or online incremental learning?
options: No, Naive Bayes must always retrain from scratch
Yes, using `partial_fit()`, Naive Bayes can incrementally update its counts, means, and variances with new batches without retraining on old data
Only if the dataset is stored in SQL
quiz.explanation: Because parameter estimation is based on summary statistics (counts and sums), incremental updating via `partial_fit()` is trivial.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of predicting a single sample in Naive Bayes across $K$ classes and $D$ features?
quiz.explanation: Inference requires evaluating $D$ feature likelihoods for each of the $K$ classes: $O(K \cdot D)$ (extremely fast).

quiz.question: Does Naive Bayes suffer from the curse of dimensionality as severely as KNN?
options: Yes, it is identical to KNN
No, because Naive Bayes evaluates features independently in 1D slices rather than computing high-dimensional spatial distances
Naive Bayes cannot run in more than 3 dimensions
quiz.explanation: Because Naive Bayes factorizes into 1D conditional likelihoods, it avoids calculating spatial distances in sparse high-dimensional space.

quiz.question: Why are predicted probabilities from Naive Bayes often poorly calibrated (extreme, pushed toward 0 or 1)?
options: Because the algorithm has a bug
The independence assumption multiplies correlated evidence multiple times, artificially inflating confidence toward certainty
Because Gaussian distributions cannot produce probabilities
Because Laplace smoothing forces probabilities to 1
quiz.explanation: Violation of independence causes correlated features to multiply evidence redundantly, driving outputs to extreme 0.00001 or 0.99999.

quiz.question: What method is recommended if accurate, calibrated probabilities are required from a Naive Bayes model?
options: Increasing the training set size by 10x
Applying post-hoc probability calibration using Platt Scaling (CalibratedClassifierCV) or Isotonic Regression
quiz.explanation: `CalibratedClassifierCV` maps raw uncalibrated Naive Bayes scores into true calibrated posterior probabilities.

quiz.question: What is the memory footprint of a trained Gaussian Naive Bayes model with $K$ classes and $D$ features?
options: $O(K \cdot D)$ to store the mean and variance for each class-feature pair
quiz.explanation: Gaussian NB only stores $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ for each feature across $K$ classes: $2 \times K \times D$ numbers (tiny memory footprint).

quiz.question: In text classification, what is the 'vocabulary' $|V|$ in Multinomial Naive Bayes?
options: The number of sentences in the training set
The total count of unique distinct words across all training documents
The dictionary size of the English language
The number of parameters in the GPU
quiz.explanation: The vocabulary $|V|$ represents the set of all unique tokens recognized by the feature extractor (e.g. CountVectorizer).

quiz.question: If word 'urgent' appears 20 times in 1,000 spam words, what is the raw unsmoothed $P(\text{'urgent'} | \text{Spam})$?
quiz.explanation: Raw likelihood is $\frac{\text{Count}}{\text{Total}} = \frac{20}{1000} = 0.02$.

quiz.question: What happens to Laplace smoothing when $\alpha$ is set extremely large (e.g. $\alpha \rightarrow \infty$)?
options: All feature likelihoods converge toward a uniform distribution $\frac{1}{|V|}$, completely washing out all empirical training data
The model weights diverge to infinity
The code throws a division by zero error
quiz.explanation: An excessively large $\alpha$ overpowers empirical counts, pushing all likelihoods toward uniform probabilities.

quiz.question: What is Lidstone smoothing in Naive Bayes?
options: Additive smoothing where hyperparameter $\alpha$ is set to a fraction between 0 and 1 (e.g. $\alpha = 0.1$), often outperforming standard Laplace $\alpha = 1.0$
quiz.explanation: Lidstone smoothing generalizes Laplace smoothing with fractional $\alpha < 1.0$, adding less aggressive pseudocounts.

quiz.question: Why is Naive Bayes often used as a baseline model in natural language processing (NLP)?
options: Because it was the first algorithm ever written
It is exceptionally fast to train, requires minimal memory, has zero complex hyperparameters, and sets a strong benchmark for text tasks
Because it is more complex than transformers
quiz.explanation: Naive Bayes establishes a rapid, reliable text benchmark in seconds before investing compute in transformer models.

quiz.question: What is the effect of class imbalance on Naive Bayes classification?
options: The prior probability $P(y)$ of the majority class dominates the posterior, biasing predictions toward the majority class
The model becomes 100% accurate on the minority class
quiz.explanation: Because $P(y)$ scales the posterior, high prior frequency shifts decision boundaries in favor of the majority class.

quiz.question: How can you mitigate class imbalance in Naive Bayes?
options: By setting uniform class priors (`fit_prior=False`) or using Complement Naive Bayes
quiz.explanation: Disabling empirical priors (`fit_prior=False`) prevents majority frequency from overwhelming likelihood signals.

quiz.question: Which of the following problems is LEAST suitable for Naive Bayes?
options: Predicting complex interaction effects where the meaning of a feature completely reverses based on another feature ($x_1 \text{ XOR } x_2$)
quiz.explanation: Because Naive Bayes assumes independent features, it is fundamentally incapable of modeling XOR interaction effects.

quiz.question: What is the denominator $P(\mathbf{x})$ in Bayes' Theorem called, and why can it be ignored when finding the predicted class $\hat{y}$?
options: It is the marginal evidence; because it is identical for all classes $y$ for a given query $\mathbf{x}$, it does not change the $\arg\max$ ranking
It is the prior; it cannot be ignored
quiz.explanation: The marginal evidence $P(\mathbf{x})$ acts as a constant normalizing factor across all candidate classes for a fixed query.

quiz.question: How does Naive Bayes handle missing feature values during inference?
options: It crashes with an unhandled exception
Because features are independent, it simply omits the missing feature from the likelihood product calculation
It imputes zero for all values
quiz.explanation: Conditional independence allows the algorithm to cleanly skip missing feature terms in the product: $\prod_{j \notin \text{missing}} P(x_j | y)$.

quiz.question: What is a typical practical application of Gaussian Naive Bayes in industry?
options: Real-time biometric sensor fault detection from continuous voltage readings
quiz.explanation: Gaussian NB is effective for rapid real-time telemetry and sensor classification with continuous numeric measurements.

quiz.question: What is the difference between BernoulliNB and MultinomialNB in text processing?
options: BernoulliNB only cares whether a word appeared at least once in a document; MultinomialNB accounts for how many times the word occurred
BernoulliNB is for regression; MultinomialNB is for classification
BernoulliNB uses GPU; MultinomialNB uses CPU
quiz.explanation: BernoulliNB binarizes term occurrences (presence/absence); MultinomialNB models term frequency counts.

quiz.question: Why does Naive Bayes require very little hyperparameter tuning?
options: Because it has millions of parameters
Its core parameters (counts, means, variances) are computed directly from closed-form statistics, leaving only the smoothing parameter $\alpha$ to tune
Because it is an unsupervised algorithm
Because it only runs on 1 epoch
quiz.explanation: Naive Bayes requires no optimization loops; tuning is typically restricted to evaluating a few smoothing values $\alpha$.

quiz.question: In a spam classification model, if $P(\text{Spam}) = 0.1$, $P(\text{'winner'} | \text{Spam}) = 0.5$, and $P(\text{'winner'} | \text{Ham}) = 0.01$, with $P(\text{Ham}) = 0.9$, which class has the higher posterior numerator for document 'winner'?
quiz.explanation: Spam score = $0.1 \times 0.5 = 0.05$; Ham score = $0.9 \times 0.01 = 0.009$. Spam is over 5x higher!
